Jim Elliot
JIM EL-ee-uht
proper noun (person)
American missionary (1927-1956) martyred with four companions by the Waorani people of Ecuador.

Biblical Definition

Jim Elliot was an American missionary to Ecuador, one of five young men martyred in 1956 in an attempt to bring the gospel to the Waorani (then called Auca), an isolated and violent people of the Ecuadorian rainforest. A man of fervent devotion from his college years, he had written in his journal the words that became his epitaph and a watchword for missions: "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose." With Nate Saint, Ed McCully, Peter Fleming, and Roger Youderian, he made contact with the Waorani and was speared to death on a sandbar of the Curaray River, the five men choosing not to use their guns against those they had come to save. Their deaths, far from ending the mission, stirred a wave of missionary commitment around the world; and through the continued labors of Elliot's widow Elisabeth and Nate Saint's sister Rachel, many of the very people who killed them came to faith in Christ. Elliot stands in the dictionary as a martyr of the modern missionary movement, whose surrender of all he could not keep, to gain what he could not lose, has called a generation to count their lives nothing for the sake of reaching the unreached with the gospel.

Webster 1828 Definition

American missionary (1927-1956) martyred with four companions by the Waorani of Ecuador; whose journal words, "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose," and whose death stirred a generation to missions.

JIM ELLIOT, proper noun. American missionary (1927-1956) to Ecuador.

One of five young men martyred in 1956 reaching the Waorani (Auca) people.

Wrote: "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose."

Speared to death on the Curaray River, refusing to fire on his attackers.

His death stirred worldwide missions; many Waorani later came to Christ.

Key Scripture

Mark 8:36 — "For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?"

Phil 3:8 — "Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,"

Rev 12:11 — "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death."

John 12:25 — "He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal."

Modern Corruption

Elliot's life honors the recovery of the eternal calculus of discipleship — spending what cannot be kept to gain what cannot be lost — against a worldly wisdom that hoards this life and counts such sacrifice insane.

expand to see more

Worldly-wisdom correction. The world counts it madness to risk one's life to reach a hostile and obscure people. Elliot reckoned by an eternal arithmetic: "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose." The dictionary holds the Savior's own logic: what shall it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his soul (Mark 8:36)? The believer who spends his perishable life for Christ's imperishable kingdom has made the wisest of all exchanges.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is overcoming by not loving one's life unto death. Elliot and his companions died as the martyrs of old, who overcame by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, loving not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11). The dictionary commends their witness: the seed of the church is the blood of the martyrs, and the death of these five young men, far from defeat, became a summons that sent a generation to the ends of the earth.
